court: New York Common Pleas, Special Term
holding_summary: The court enjoined application of the hotel lodging-room water charge because the building was not a hotel and water could not be supplied to all of its rooms. It nevertheless stated that a large lodging house freely supplied with water could fall within the ordinance.

quotes.text: This is an application for an injimction to restrain the Croton Aqueduct Board from cutting off the Croton water from a large building at the corner of Frankfort and William streets, owned by the plaintiff, which is used as a cheap lodging-house.

While, therefore, I am disposed to think that a large lodging-house, to which water is freely supplied, would come within the intention of the ordinance, I am of the opinion that the plaintiff’s building does not.

It is a case, in my judgment, coming under the portion of the ordinance which provides that matters not mentioned are to- be arranged by a special contract, and not under the one which imposes a charge upon each lodging-room. I shall, therefore, grant the injunction.

notes: The establishment contained 180 rooms let at twenty-five cents per night; the result was favorable to this operator, but the court indicated that the ordinance could cover other large lodging houses.

In this the justice erred. The statute is open to criticism, it is true; and construed according to its letter, would defeat the intention of the legislature, and warrant the decision which the justice made in this case.

holding_summary: An operator who let rooms without providing meals was a lodging-house keeper rather than an innkeeper, despite an independently managed restaurant in the basement. Mere lodging-house keepers had no lien on their lodgers' effects.

The act which provides for the protection of boarding house keepers, (Laws of 1860, p. 771,) gives the lien upon the effects of the boarders for the amount which may be due for board, and it cannot be extended to any other indebtedness, nor to any demand not due at the time of the detention.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: A hotel occupant paying a weekly room rate without agreeing to remain for a particular time was an innkeeper's guest, not merely a boarder or lodger. The judgment for the hotel operator concerning the occupant's unexplained property loss was reversed.

quotes.text: We are of opinion that the relationship of innkeeper and guest existed between the parties.

The common law holds the innkeeper absolutely liable for all thefts from within, or unexplained losses of property in his charge, belonging, to his guest, although he may be discharged from liability by any contributory negligence of the guest.

It does not appear that the plaintiff bargained to remain for any particular time, although it is true that the agreed price of the room was to be $1.25 per week. But a special agreement fixing in advance the price to be paid, or the length of the stay, does not absolutely disturb the relation of innkeeper and guest, and constitute the person so acting a boarder or lodger.

notes: The weekly price did not establish the occupant's actual length of stay, so duration is unclear.

holding_summary: A boarding-house keeper was required to exercise ordinary and reasonable care for a boarder's goods and was liable for a loss caused by a servant's negligence within the scope of employment.

quotes.text: It appears, from the evidence, that the defendant is a boarding and lodging-house keeper, and that the plaintiff had been boarding and lodging with him for some time prior to the 20th day of March, 1873.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: The defendant's licensing affidavit established that his combined restaurant and lodging establishment was an inn. He was therefore liable as an innkeeper for a dining guest's coat lost inside the establishment, despite the slight and temporary character of the entertainment.

quotes.text: But the difficulty, in the present case, is, that the defendant himself has established, by his own act and declaration, that he keeps an inn, having obtained, upon an affidavit made by him for that purpose, a license to sell spirituous liquors upon the premises, which he could not have obtained unless upon proof by affidavit to the board of commissioners of excise that he kept an inn, and that an inn was necessary for the accommodation of travelers in the place where he kept it (Laws of 1857, c. 628).

If it was an inn, the defendant was answerable for the loss of the coat whilst the plaintiff was taking his dinner, and as the judge below held that it was, I do not see how we can say that he erred, when the facts sworn to in the defendant’s affidavit show that it was.

But the difficulty, in the present case, is, that the defendant himself has established, by his own act and declaration, that he keeps an inn, having obtained, upon an affidavit made by him for that purpose, a license to sell spirituous liquors upon the premises, which he could not have obtained unless upon proof by affidavit to the board of commissioners of excise that he kept an inn, and that an inn was necessary for the accommodation of travelers in the place where he kept it (Laws of 1857, c. 628).

Where it appears by the defendant’s own showing that the establishment he keeps, is an inn, it is immaterial how slight may be the entertainment or how temporary the use made of it, if the party loses his property in the inn while there in the character of a guest.

notes: Mixed because the court protected the guest through innkeeper liability while treating the operator's license representations as establishing a regulated inn. The plaintiff only ate a meal and did not occupy a lodging room, so occupancy duration is unclear.

holding_summary: A boarding-house keeper must exercise reasonable care for a boarder's property and is liable when a servant acting within the scope of employment negligently enables its theft.

court: New York Common Pleas, General Term
holding_summary: The 1860 statute gave boarding-house keepers an innkeeper-like lien for unpaid board without distinguishing between transient and permanent boarders. The court described boarding-house accommodation as ordinarily furnished for a definite weekly or monthly period at an agreed rate.

quotes.text: A boarding-house keeper, as contradistinguished from the keeper of an inn, should, in the sense of this statute, be regarded as one who furnishes accommodation for a definite period, as by the week or month, at a rate of compensation agreed upon.

The intent of the statute of 1860, (Sess, Laws, 771,) giving to the keeper of a boarding house a lien to the extent of the board due, is, to give them the same lien which an inn-keeper has upon the effects of a guest, without reference to the character of the guests, whether they are transient ox permanent boarders.

A boarding-house keeper, as contradistinguished from the keeper of an inn, should, in the sense of this statute, be regarded as one who furnishes accommodation for a definite period, as by the week or month, at a rate of compensation agreed upon.

Before the passage of this statute this class, now a very numerous one, had no lien upon the effects of the persons to whom they supplied entertainment, and it was evidently the intent of this statute to give them the same lien which an inn-keeper has upon the effects of a guest.

notes: The court classified the relationship as boarding for an agreed period and price rather than as a lease, license, or innkeeping arrangement, so characterization is other. The particular boarder's actual duration is not given.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: A family occupying hotel rooms for an anticipated period of several months remained in the relation of guests to the innkeepers despite an express agreement fixing the price and probable duration. The innkeepers were consequently liable for property stolen from the rooms.

quotes.text: We are of the opinion that the facts of this case establish clearly the relation of innkeeper and guest.

We cannot adopt the theory that ascertaining and fixing the price which was to be paid for the accommodations, and specifying the probable duration of the stay at the hotel, necessarily had the effect to deprive the plaintiff of the character of guest.

A careful examination of this case has convinced us that, upon the facts found by the referee, the plaintiff should! have been regarded the guest of the defendants at their hotel, and as such entitled to recover the value of her property, which was, stolen from the room occupied by her in such hotel.

We cannot subscribe to the doctrine, which refuses to recognize as a guest a visitor at a hotel who occupies rooms and is furnished meals therein by the proprietor; simply because the agreement which the law implies between innkeeper and guest is amplifier! by an express stipulation which fixes the price ; and specifies the duration of the stay of the guest.

notes: The family occupied the rooms from November 1873 until about June 12, 1874. The operator was a public hotel rather than a householder letting part of a private dwelling.

holding_summary: The court classified Mrs. Morris as one who rented rooms to lodgers rather than a boarding-house keeper. Consequently, she had no statutory hotel or boarding-house lien on the lodger's personal property; the assault conviction was reversed on a separate jury-instruction issue.

It seems to us clear that the buildings in question are a boarding house. They are used by one tenant for a single purpose. They have interior communications with each other, and the dining room and parlor in one building serve the purpose of those common rooms for the boarders in both buildings.

court: Pa. Court of Common Pleas, Allegheny County
holding_summary: The court held that tourist homes and coffee houses fell within the ordinance's residential-district exception for renting rooms or lodgings and serving meals for compensation. Because the council imposed no limit on the number of rooms rented or meals served, the requested mandamus compelling zoning enforcement was dismissed.

quotes.text: And as to the use of a sign, this court has already held that it would be “an accessory use to the permitted use of operating a house for the renting of rooms and serving of meals to the public.”
Certainly tourist homes involve “the renting of rooms or lodgings,” and “the serving of meals for compensation,” and it seems to us that is all they do involve.

Had the council intended to set a limitation of any sort either upon the number of rooms of a dwelling which could be rented or the number of meals which could be served at any one time, it was within its power to do so, but it did not see fit to exercise that power.

It is our opinion that tourist homes and coffee houses of the type generally referred to by counsel for the parties fall under the head of “Use District Exceptions” by the provision, “In the residence districts the use regulations shall not be held to prevent the renting of rooms or lodgings or the serving of meals for compensation.”
